papers.title: Beyond neuroinflammation: α-synuclein as a molecular bridge and organizer of immune communication networks in Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Song X, Wang X, Zhang K.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as involving not only α-synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation, but also complex immune dysregulation that cannot be fully explained by individual inflammatory pathways. Here, we propose a communication network-based framework in which extracellular α-synuclein acts as a neuronal pathology-derived signal that initiates multicellular immune communication. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, together with ligand-receptor inference, provide new opportunities to reconstruct these networks by resolving disease-associated cellular states, spatial organization and intercellular signaling. This perspective shifts current models from isolated receptor activation toward network reorganization across the neuroimmune microenvironment. Importantly, this framework offers immunologists a roadmap to move beyond neuroinflammation as a black-box endpoint, toward mechanistic understanding of how immune recognition of neuron-derived signals reorganizes tissue-level communication architecture. Accordingly, future therapies may benefit from targeting disease-associated communication networks in a stage- and context-dependent manner rather than broadly suppressing neuroinflammation or individual pathways. We hypothesize that α-synuclein does more than trigger inflammation: by engaging different receptors on different cells, it may shape the wiring of the communication network itself-which signals are amplified, which are lost, and how the network changes over time. Treating α-synuclein as the starter of molecular immune communication networks is a feasible way to study the pathogenesis of PD and to develop specific therapeutic measures.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: Schematic comparison of the receptor-centric model and the α-synuclein-driven communication network model in Parkinson’s disease, with evidence-level annotations. Evidence key: [S] supported by human tissue/fluid data and/or multiple independent experimental systems; [MS] demonstrated mainly in cell, organoid, overexpression, α-synuclein preformed fibril, or animal models, or inferred from well-established pathway homology; [H] mechanistically plausible but still lacking direct in vivo /human evidence. These tags annotate the evidentiary status of the mechanistic statements in this legend, not the individual graphical arrows. (Left) The receptor-centric model posits that extracellular α-synuclein engages individual immune receptors on microglia and other glial cells. Extracellular α-synuclein can signal through TLR2 and, in a conformation-dependent manner, TLR4, with oligomeric species generally reported as more potent TLR2 agonists than monomers [MS]. TLR4 engagement can activate NF-κB-dependent inflammatory programs [S for the canonical TLR4–NF-κB pathway; MS for α-synuclein as the disease-relevant ligand], whereas microglial TLR4–NF-κB–p62/SQSTM1 signaling has also been linked to selective autophagic/synucleinphagic clearance rather than solely to inflammation [MS]. MHC-II-mediated presentation of α-synuclein peptides to CD4+ T cells is supported in experimental systems and by peripheral T-cell reactivity in PD patients [S/MS], whereas direct demonstration of microglial antigen presentation to T cells within the human PD brain remains limited [H]. Thus, this model is best viewed as a useful reduction of localized uptake, clearance, inflammatory, and repair signals, rather than a complete account of multicellular propagation or network reorganization. (Right) The α-synuclein-driven communication network model proposes that pathological α-synuclein sensing is an initiating event that recruits secondary signals—TNF-α, IL-1β, CCL2, other cytokines/chemokines, and DAMPs—and redistributes information across neurons, microglia, astrocytes, macrophage-like cells, and T cells [MS for individual edges; H for the integrated topology]. Microglial recognition/endocytosis of α-synuclein and reactive astrogliosis are experimentally supported components [MS], whereas reciprocal IFN/T-cell feedback, microglial state transitions toward antigen-presentation-like phenotypes, and astrocyte rewiring remain plausible but incompletely resolved in human disease [H/MS]. In this framework, α-synuclein may bias which signaling edges are amplified or silenced; however, the stronger claim that it actively “orchestrates” the emergent wiring topology should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an established principle [H]. DAMP, damage-associated molecular pattern; IFN, interferon; MHC-II, major histocompatibility complex class II; TLR, Toll-like receptor; TNF, tumor necrosis factor.

papers.title: Premalignant immune remodeling in laryngeal carcinogenesis: a framework to define when immune interception becomes testable.
papers.authors: Hong WZ, Long CQ, Lu BQ.
papers.abstract: Laryngeal dysplasia presents a clinical dilemma because lesions with similar histology can have different outcomes. Single-cell, spatial and pathology studies show immune remodeling before invasion, yet differences between lesion stages do not establish future progression risk within dysplasia. We consider three potentially coexisting explanations of a premalignant immune signal, namely reactive recruitment, ineffective antitumor activity and a stromal niche that supports progression. Each requires different spatial and functional evidence. We adapt established validation principles to five evidence requirements concerning lesion identity, future invasion, spatial and functional state, causal reversibility and clinical readiness. Their purpose is to separate risk stratification from target validation, rather than require one marker to perform both roles. Existing laryngeal studies address parts of this framework, but none establishes that targeting a premalignant immune circuit prevents cancer. The immediate priority is to compare histologically comparable lesions with known outcomes and test candidate interactions in models that retain noninvasive epithelium. Short window studies may subsequently establish target engagement and biological activity, but clinical prevention requires separate evidence of reduced invasive cancer risk and acceptable harm.

figure.label: Figure 1
figure.caption: Evidence requirements for testing immune interception in laryngeal premalignancy. (A) Endoscopic vocal fold leukoplakia does not establish histological dysplasia. Clinically indicated biopsy may identify dysplastic epithelium with an intact basement membrane. Three potentially coexisting interpretations of premalignant immune remodeling are illustrated, including reactive recruitment, ineffective antitumor activity and a candidate progression-supportive epithelial, immune and stromal niche. These interpretations remain hypotheses rather than established causal mechanisms. (B) Two complementary evidence streams distinguish risk assessment from mechanistic validation. Risk evidence links well-defined lesions to subsequent invasive cancer under documented care to support population selection and prognostic validation. Mechanistic evidence combines spatial and functional characterization with targeted perturbation in noninvasive precursor models to assess candidate dependencies. The streams may proceed in parallel, and the risk marker need not be the intervention target. (C) Clinical readiness requires an appropriate population, a defensible target and acceptable harm. Short window studies before planned excision may assess target engagement, biological activity and safety without delaying necessary treatment. These findings may inform subsequent controlled prevention studies but cannot establish preventive efficacy. Demonstrating cancer prevention requires invasive cancer outcomes, adequate follow-up and assessment of voice, airway function and immune toxicity. All curves are illustrative, and arrows indicate proposed research decisions rather than established causal relationships. No preventive benefit has been demonstrated in laryngeal dysplasia.

papers.title: A Nitrated T-Cell Epitope Enhances the Antitumor Immune Response of a TOPK-Targeted Vaccine in Glioblastoma and Its Potential for Remodeling the Tumor Microenvironment.
papers.authors: Deng D, Shi Y, Wu G, Zhang W, Qian Q, Tian H, Peng Y.
papers.abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains the most lethal primary brain tumor in adults, largely due to recurrence after surgery. Cancer vaccines, which can activate a patient's adaptive immune system against specific tumor antigens, are a promising strategy for improving outcomes in patients with GBM. Methods: We examined the function of T-lymphokine-activated killer cell-originated protein kinase (TOPK), a candidate tumor-associated antigen, in GBM. We then constructed TOPK-NitraTh, a vaccine coupled to a nitrated T-cell epitope (NitraTh) and targeting TOPK. Its efficacy was evaluated in the GL261 orthotopic GBM model, and single-cell RNA sequencing was used to explore the underlying immune mechanisms. Results: TOPK functioned as a tumor-promoting factor in GBM. Vaccination with TOPK-NitraTh elicited TOPK-specific adaptive immune responses and inhibited GBM progression in the GL261 orthotopic model. Exploratory single-cell RNA sequencing analysis led us to hypothesize that the NitraTh-based vaccine may reprogram macrophages potentially via the NF-κB signaling pathway, potentially contributing to the reversal of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Conclusions: Given its ability to remodel the tumor microenvironment, the NitraTh-based vaccine represents a promising preclinical strategy for GBM treatment.

papers.title: SERPINB5 and SPAG6 as candidate correlates of the molecular pathology of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: integrated bioinformatics and in vivo evidence.
papers.authors: Li S, Li P, Liu J, Zhang W, Zhu C, Wang C, Zhang H, Xia Q, Zhang H, Zhang Y.
papers.abstract: Objective This study aims to elucidate the molecular pathology of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) by identifying key genes associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) organization and remodeling, and immune dysregulation. Methods Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified from three Gene Expression Omnibus datasets (GSE110147, GSE21369, GSE24206) using limma and robust rank aggregation (RRA). Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction network analyses were performed to prioritize hub genes. Diagnostic potential was assessed via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves in an independent cohort (GSE32537; 119 patients with IPF and 50 healthy controls), with bootstrap optimism correction and repeated cross-validation. Immune infiltration was quantified using CIBERSORT and cross-validated by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA). Preliminary validation was performed in a bleomycin-induced murine model using Western blotting, quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and immunofluorescence. Results 409 robust DEGs were identified, significantly enriched in ECM organization and ciliary structure and motility. CDH2 , HYDIN , MMP13 , SERPINB5 , SERPINF1 , and SPAG6 were established as hub genes, demonstrating strong diagnostic performance (individual-gene AUCs ranging from 0.832 to 0.951, combined AUC = 0.981; bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC = 0.971). IPF tissues exhibited altered immune landscapes, characterized by diminished M1 macrophage infiltration. SERPINB5 and SPAG6 exhibited significant negative correlations with M1 macrophage signatures (ρ = -0.41 and -0.46, respectively). In vivo , both genes were significantly upregulated in fibrotic lung tissues and showed qualitative colocalization with macrophage markers. Cross-validation by ssGSEA independently reproduced the diminished M1 macrophage signature and the negative SERPINB5 / SPAG6 -M1 correlations. Conclusion SERPINB5 and SPAG6 are identified herein as candidate correlates of the molecular pathology of IPF. Their association with ECM remodeling and M1 macrophage polarization is consistent with a functionally relevant role within the fibrotic network. These results provide a foundation for future functional studies aimed at elucidating their precise roles in pulmonary fibrosis.

papers.title: mRNA-based cancer vaccines for cancer immunotherapy: current progress, challenges, and emerging opportunities.
papers.authors: Kulshreshtha S, Kumar U, Uddandrao VVS, Singh S, Mandloi A, Gogoi H.
papers.abstract: mRNA-based cancer vaccines have emerged as a promising platform for therapeutic cancer immunotherapy because of their ability to encode tumor-associated antigens, tumor-specific antigens, and patient-specific neoantigens and to induce antigen-specific immune responses. Their flexible and cell-free manufacturing enables rapid adaptation and facilitates the development of personalized vaccines based on individual tumor mutations and HLA profiles. However, the clinical translation of mRNA-based cancer vaccines remains challenging because of difficulties in neoantigen identification, maintaining mRNA stability, achieving efficient intracellular and tissue-specific delivery and endosomal escape, optimizing antigen expression, and overcoming tumor heterogeneity, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments. Advances in mRNA engineering, including sequence optimization, modified nucleosides, cap and UTR optimization, and lipid nanoparticle-based delivery, have improved RNA stability, cellular uptake, antigen expression, and immune activation in various experimental and clinical settings. This review discusses the principles of mRNA-based cancer vaccines, strategies for neoantigen identification and vaccine development, mRNA production and formulation, nanoparticle-mediated delivery, major challenges affecting stability, targeting, expression, and immune stimulation, and emerging clinical applications. Particular emphasis is placed on personalized neoantigen vaccines and combination approaches with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Continued integration of RNA engineering, nanotechnology, computational antigen prediction, and precision immunotherapy may enable more effective and clinically adaptable mRNA-based cancer vaccines.

papers.title: In Silico-Guided Screening of a High-Affinity PD-L1 Aptamer for the Construction of a Sensitive Electrochemical Aptasensor.
papers.authors: Zha L, Pang X, Gui Z, Wang H, Jin X, Wang F.
papers.abstract: Programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an essential immune checkpoint protein that plays a pivotal role in tumor immune evasion and has emerged as an important biomarker for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and immunotherapy monitoring. Aptamers have attracted increasing attention as promising molecular recognition elements owing to their high specificity, excellent chemical stability, and facile synthesis. In this study, we developed an in silico-guided aptamer screening strategy that integrates virtual library construction, molecular docking, secondary structure prediction, and structural interaction analysis to identify high-affinity PD-L1-binding aptamers, yielding a dissociation constant (Kd) of 20.73 nM. Based on the optimized aptamer, a reduced graphene oxide (rGO)-modified screen-printed electrode was fabricated to construct a label-free electrochemical aptasensor. The developed aptasensor exhibited a wide linear detection range from 0.01 to 100 nM, with a detection limit of 0.0074 nM. Moreover, the biosensor demonstrated excellent selectivity, satisfactory reproducibility, and good storage stability. The combination of computational aptamer screening with electrochemical sensing provides an efficient strategy for developing high-performance aptamer biosensors and offers considerable potential for rapid PD-L1 determination in clinical liquid biopsy and cancer immunotherapy monitoring.

papers.title: Integrated Plasma Proteomic and Single-Cell Transcriptomic Profiling of Three COVID-19 Second-Booster Regimens: An Exploratory Analysis of a Randomized Phase IV Trial.
papers.authors: Wang W, Zheng H, Jin P, Wu T, Qiao Q, Zhu X, Tang R, Wei M, Jia S, Li L, Xu M, Li J.
papers.abstract: Background Waning vaccine-induced immunity and the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants have prompted the evaluation of alternative booster strategies. We investigated the systemic immune profiles associated with three second-booster regimens in adults previously vaccinated with three doses of an inactivated vaccine. Methods This exploratory analysis was nested within a randomized phase IV trial comparing homologous CoronaVac (ICV), intramuscular Ad5-nCoV (IM), and inhaled Ad5-nCoV (IH) boosting. Serum antibody responses were assessed, 119 plasma samples underwent Olink inflammatory-protein profiling, and 24 peripheral blood mononuclear cell samples were analyzed by single-cell RNA sequencing. Results At Day 14, wild-type SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibody geometric mean titers were 880.8, 297.6, and 77.3 in the IM, IH, and ICV groups, respectively. Seven inflammatory proteins were upregulated in both Ad5-nCoV groups, and several were positively associated with antibody responses. In the small scRNA-seq subset, the IH group showed a higher observed peripheral CD8 + T cell proportion than the IM and ICV groups, together with antigen presentation- and cytotoxicity-related transcriptional patterns; neither vaccine-specific lymphocyte responses nor cellular function was directly measured. Conclusions The three booster regimens were associated with distinct Day 14 humoral, inflammatory protein, and peripheral immune cell profiles. These hypothesis-generating observations complement the immunogenicity findings of the parent trial but do not establish a causal mechanism or identify a clinically preferred booster regimen.

papers.title: Granzyme K+CD8 T cells exacerbate renal inflammation and fibrosis in chronic kidney disease.
papers.authors: Tang W, Deng S, Yu J, Zhuang X, Zhou H, Yu C, Hu Y.
papers.abstract: Renal inflammation is a hallmark pathological feature of chronic kidney disease (CKD). Granzyme K (GZMK)-expressing T cells have been implicated in diverse inflammatory disorders, yet their role in CKD remains unclear. By analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), we found a significant enrichment of Gzmk+ T cells in both human and murine CKD kidneys. Further evaluation identified renal CD8 T cells as the primary source of Gzmk, with a smaller contribution from CD4 T cells. Genetic ablation of Gzmk in mice attenuated renal inflammation and fibrosis following bilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury, without substantially affecting the severity of the initial ischemic injury. In fibrotic kidneys, Gzmk deficiency was associated with reduced accumulation and activation of renal T cells, as well as with attenuated macrophage inflammatory responses. Further scRNA-seq analysis identified a potential differentiation trajectory from Tcf7+ naïve/central memory T-like cells through effector memory T-like cells toward the Gzmk+ CD8 T cell state. Cell-cell communication analysis identified predicted interactions of GZMK+ CD8 T cells with macrophages and fibroblasts, with CXCL16-CXCR6 emerging as a prominent candidate pathway for macrophage-CD8 T cell communication. Spatial analysis further demonstrated frequent proximity between renal CD8 T cells and macrophages in injured kidneys. Together, these findings identify GZMK+ CD8 T cells as a pathogenic immune population that contributes to sustained renal inflammation and fibrosis following kidney injury, potentially through modulation of T cell and macrophage inflammatory responses.

papers.title: COMSOL-Based Impedance and Sensitivity Analysis of an Interdigitated Electrode Biosensor for Dengue NS1 Detection.
papers.authors: Alzahrani SI.
papers.abstract: Dengue remains a major global public health concern, highlighting the need for rapid and sensitive methods for the early detection of dengue virus biomarkers. In the present study, a finite element model for the detection of dengue nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) using an interdigitated electrode (IDE)-based impedimetric biosensor was developed in COMSOL Multiphysics. The proposed sensor consists of gold IDEs coated with an antibody-based biorecognition layer and immersed in a conductive aqueous sample medium. Antibody-NS1 binding was modeled using the Langmuir adsorption isotherm. Frequency-domain simulations were used to examine the impedance response over a range of NS1 concentrations from 0 to 1000 ng/cm 3 . The results showed that the simulated impedance magnitude decreased with increasing NS1 concentration and excitation frequency. At 10 MHz, the normalized impedance response increased rapidly at low NS1 concentrations and gradually approached saturation at higher concentrations. A linear fit to three simulated concentration points (1-3 ng/cm 3 ) yielded a normalized response slope of 0.9223%/(ng/cm 3 ) (R 2 = 0.9963), providing a preliminary characterization of the model-predicted low-concentration response. These findings demonstrate the potential of computational modeling for characterizing the predicted electrical response of an IDE-based impedimetric NS1 biosensor, providing a basis for sensor optimization and future experimental validation. The reported sensitivity and concentration-dependent responses are simulation-based predictions and have not been experimentally validated.

papers.title: Computational image features of immune architecture reveal molecular patterns associated with outcome and risk of recurrence in microsatellite-stable or MSI-low colon cancers
papers.authors: Song B, Maurya H, Khalighi S, Aqeel A, Corredor G, Hammouda K, Ozyoruk K, Pathak T, Toro P, Chen C, Fu P, Zhao K, Lu C, Wang X, Willis J, Madabhushi A.

papers.title: Intratumoral Therapeutic Injections for Lung Cancer: Current Evidence, Personalized Therapeutic Approaches, and Future Directions.
papers.authors: Maser T, Bani Salem M, Al Zoubi O, Iakovidis A, Castro M, Chen J, Patel P, Vijayan K, Mehta HJ.
papers.abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide despite significant advances in surgery, radiation therapy, targeted therapies, and immunotherapy. Although systemic therapies have improved outcomes across all stages of disease, treatment efficacy is often limited by inadequate intratumoral drug delivery, systemic toxicities, treatment resistance, and disease heterogeneity. Intratumoral therapeutic injections (ITIs), including intratumoral chemotherapy (ITC), have emerged as a promising locoregional therapeutic strategy designed to overcome these limitations through direct delivery of antineoplastic agents into tumor tissue. Advances in bronchoscopic technologies, particularly endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle injection (EBUS-TBNI), robotic bronchoscopy, electromagnetic navigation bronchoscopy, and cone-beam computed tomography guidance, have expanded the feasibility of delivering therapeutic agents to central and peripheral pulmonary lesions. Most of the evidence for ITI comes from case reports, prospective or retrospective studies with small sample sizes, and non-randomized, single-arm clinical trials. While further evidence is needed, especially in the form of randomized controlled trials, the current literature shows promise in the areas of malignant airway obstruction and isolated mediastinal and hilar recurrence. Studies have also assessed the utility of novel formulations, including large surface area microparticle paclitaxel (LSAM-PTX). Potential future applications of ITI include use as neoadjuvant therapy, as part of combination therapy with radiation and immune checkpoint inhibitors, and in cases of oligoprogressive disease and medically inoperable tumors. Novel formulations, including large surface area microparticle paclitaxel (LSAM-PTX), sustained-release drug delivery systems, and the potential use of immunomodulatory agents, have further enhanced the therapeutic potential of local drug administration. Furthermore, advances in radiomics, artificial intelligence, computational drug distribution modeling, and biomarker-driven patient selection have positioned ITI within the broader framework of personalized cancer therapy. This review summarizes the biological rationale, technical approaches, clinical evidence, and future directions of ITI in lung cancer, emphasizing its evolving role as a precision therapeutic platform capable of providing effective cancer treatment alongside established therapeutic paradigms.

papers.title: Sustaining Antitumor Immunity: The Unmet Challenge of Durable T-Cell Responses in Cancer Vaccination.
papers.authors: Luo H, Feng Q, Wang F, Shen Z.
papers.abstract: This narrative review examines therapeutic cancer vaccines, which have undergone a profound renaissance, transitioning from early peptide and dendritic cell-based formulations to next-generation mRNA platforms enabling personalized neoantigen targeting. Despite unprecedented successes-most notably the autogene cevumeran trial in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma achieving durable CD8 + T cell responses, with a model-estimated mean clonal lifespan of 7.7 years in a small phase I trial-a fundamental "durability paradox" persists: robust peripheral T cell responses frequently fail to translate into long-term clinical benefit. This review systematically examines the immunological basis of durable antitumor immunity, the clinical evidence supporting long-lived T cell responses, and the formidable barriers imposed by the tumor microenvironment (TME). We dissect how chronic antigen exposure, metabolic competition, and epigenetic reprogramming-particularly TOX-driven exhaustion-conspire to erode memory T cell pools. We then evaluate engineering strategies to enhance durability, including optimized antigen selection (neoantigens over TAAs), rational adjuvant selection (TLR9/CD40/STING agonists), sustained-release delivery systems (LNPs, polymeric depots), prime-boost scheduling, and combinatorial approaches with immune checkpoint inhibitors and TME modulators. Finally, we discuss emerging biomarkers (TCR clonality tracking, ctDNA dynamics) and future directions, including AI-driven multi-omics modeling and neoadjuvant vaccination. The convergence of compelling decade-scale durability data-from mRNA, UV1, and WT1 peptide vaccines-with next-generation engineering platforms suggests that cancer vaccines may evolve from short-term immune activators into long-term immune sentinels, provided that the dual challenges of T cell stemness preservation and TME immunosuppression are simultaneously addressed.

papers.title: Syndecan-3 couples tumor mechanics to immunosuppressive macrophage identity.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Li K, Cheng M, Chen S, Xiong G, Liu X, Ling R, Su J, Wang C, Wang CY, Chen D.
papers.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages adopt suppressive states, but how tumor stress installs these programs remains unclear. Here, we identify syndecan-3 (SDC3) as a macrophage-intrinsic mechanosensory regulator by integrating in vivo functional screening, single-cell and spatial profiling, and genetic and pharmacological perturbation. SDC3 + macrophages accumulate in hypoxic, stiff tumor niches and suppress antitumor cytotoxic T-cell responses. Matrix stiffness increases mechanical loading on SDC3, reorganizes an SDC3-associated scaffold and opens suppressive chromatin loci. This program engages a CDK7-MAFB relay to induce TREM2, which functions as a required suppressive effector in mice. Human-cell assays support a species-specific TREM2-associated inhibition mechanism. Naldemedine engages TREM2, restores cytotoxic T-cell activity, improves tumor control and enhances immune-checkpoint blockade in vivo. These findings define a targetable SDC3-CDK7-MAFB-TREM2 axis linking hypoxia and tissue mechanics to macrophage-mediated immune evasion.
